result:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but merge preserves history as it happened while rebase rewrites it to be linear.

`git merge feature` ties the two branches together with a new merge commit that has two parents, leaving every existing commit untouched. `git rebase main` (run from the feature branch) replays your commits one by one on top of main's tip, creating new commits with new hashes, so the history looks as if you had started your work from the latest main.

In practice: rebase your own local, unpushed branch to tidy it up before sharing, and merge when bringing work into a shared branch. Don't rebase commits that others have already pulled, because the rewritten hashes diverge from theirs and force them to repair their history; if you must push a rebased branch, use `git push --force-with-lease` rather than `--force`.

Conflicts also differ: merge asks you to resolve them once, while rebase may stop for resolution at each replayed commit.
